b: I have lost a couple of good friends to the conspiracy theory wormhole over the past decade. So please be assured that the following post is not a coming out party for Monevator: The Tinfoil Hat Years.
However, you have to admit things feel a little… broken.
The UK government officially advised us to stockpile three days of food.
A critical bug discovered in the PHP scripting language took countless websites offline.
US authorities issued a rare ‘stop order’ that grounded all aircraft for hours.
Supermarket freezers across Europe were compromised, trashing their contents.
A 24-hour Microsoft Teams’ outage caused chaos across the world.
The US National Security Agency’s internal communications network went down.
As I type, a critical flaw has just been discovered in the Java language.
Now, these different borkings all had varied – and probably legitimate – explanations.
The fridges fell to cyberattacks. The need to prevent similar outages lies behind the PHP drama. Elsewhere, everything from routine software patches to problems with copper wires have been fingered.

The National Security Agency says software tweaks to address vulnerabilities is what caused its own issues, and it implies similar patching also accounts for other smaller outages that I haven’t listed above, such as those seen with major US banks and Apple’s iTunes in recent days.
The truth is out there, as the X-Files once reminded us each week.
I’ve got 502 reasons and North Korea ain’t one
Occam’s Razor tells us the simplest solution is to be preferred. And the Route One explanation is that AI has made it easier to find and exploit holes in legacy software.
In some cases – such as the fridges – the baddies got there first.

Mostly though, institutions are shoring up their systems before falling to such attacks. Typically this does the trick, and we never even hear about it. But sometimes there’s a glitch, and we get planes sat on the ground or delays to the 10am all-hands Teams call. (It’s not all bad news then!)
That mundane answer wouldn’t satisfy my fringe friends though, nor Mulder and Scully.
Is it possible, rather, that in some instances a bad actor – say Russia or North Korea – has been probing and penetrating our tech defences, and the authorities don’t want us to panic?
Or is the glut of headlines a reflection not of competence by firms and institutions in the face of AI-sharpened digital warfare – but rather that things are coming apart?

Could it even be that the authorities are systematically switching these services off themselves, to test how the public responds ahead of some coup? (Wander into the darkest corners on the Internet and you’ll quickly find this theory espoused.)
My response is respectively: possible but unlikely in most instances, perhaps but probably not, and *TI backs away slowly*.
The simplest solution is very likely correct. But that doesn’t mean that a literal clusterfuck like we’ve seen recently shouldn’t give us pause.
The four horsemen of the cock-up-alypse
Whatever the specific reason(s) for these outages, SNAFUs, timeouts, and bungles, they might all lead us to question how resilient our lifestyle is.
Particularly, for Monevator purposes, our financial set-up.
Let’s do a quick whack-a-mole on each of the probable causes, beginning with an age-old issue on the Internet.
Our lives have been becoming ever more digital for decades, so online security should be familiar territory by now.
Unguessable and unique passwords are table stakes, obviously. Using password managers – whether dedicated third-party services or those that come with the likes of macOS or Chrome – is best practice.
And yes, you should have two-factor authentication turned on for anything other than your 20-year-old hobby accounts and maybe even for those.
Be careful what apps you keep on your phone, which should be biometrically protected. Do you need to be able to access your six-figure rainy day savings on the Clapham omnibus? I’d hope not.
According to some analysts, AI is ushering in an exponential increase in cyberattacks:
It’s worth remembering though that the same AI technology should also be helping legitimate companies to find vulnerabilities before they’re exposed, and so to harden their defences too.
Of course, you can fortify your own online accounts but your service provider can still be taken down by hackers.
That points to building redundancy and resilience into your set-up, which we’ll get to next.
Password managers for the Post-it generation
While I sometimes wonder what it’s done to our nervous systems, I’m generally in favour of how much we’ve offloaded to digital services and the cloud.
I prefer Apple Pay to cheques or debit cards. Uber to taxis. Emails to stamps. And Airbnb to 30 minutes with a travel agent.
The list is endless, but that also brings with it an endless number of ways in which you can find yourself banging your head against a cyber-wall when something fails.

Systems falling down or going offline are nothing new – I’ll remember to my dying days how my broker platforms blinked in and out of life at the height of the financial crisis – and perhaps their modern reliability is why outages do now make the news. I certainly haven’t seen definitive statistics showing they’re more common.
But it sure feels like the matrix is glitching a lot of late.
None of the security people I’ve talked with has predicted an apocalypse.
But they’re pretty convinced that the next 18 months are going to be a hassle, with regular disruptions to services that we rely on.

That’s because when cyber defenders find a hole they can’t patch fast enough, the rational move is to amputate: Switch the system off and wait. Big institutions already do this, more quietly and more often than you’d think.

Whatever caused today’s ground stop, halting every departure in the country ‘for reasons of safety’ until someone works out what’s going on isn’t a sign that the system is failing. More and more, it is the system.
If the operating manual at your service provider says “if in doubt, switch it off” then what’s the best response?
Backups and redundancy! Aim for at least two bank accounts, two credit cards, two investing platforms, and arguably cash somewhere about your person, even if you’ve not used paper money for years.
Be aware that some of these alternatives will share underlying systems. It’s tricky, but ideally you’d account for that, too.
Redundancy could also mean periodically printing out copies of bank and portfolio statements, in case an outage turns into something more serious.

Remember that cascading failure is a risk with any complex system. For instance if the electricity cuts off, that will suspend your digital life with it. I’m not saying everyone needs their own generator. But an always-charged power bank for your phone seems a sensible precaution.
And what if your mobile network goes down for days? Should we all have a burner SIM that sits on a different telecoms infrastructure?
Don’t forget to document all this somewhere for your loved ones, in case you’re run over by a self-driving bus should its hive brain go on the blink.
In The Revenge of the Shallow State, US academic Daniel Drezner suggests the dismantling of failsafes and redundancy by Trump zealots has exacerbated fragility in the US:
The more we learn about what DOGE hath wrought the bigger the shitstorm that emerges.

A reformer genuinely interested in improving government efficiency would have found ways to eliminate cumbersome regulations while maintaining the workforce to adroitly administer the remaining rules and services. DOGE did the exact opposite, firing employees without simplifying government tasks.
Has the infrastructure of US civil society been hollowed out by a recklessly destructive Trump regime? It seems plausible to me, though naturally I have my biases.

I mean, it’s not like we haven’t seen issues here, too. I’ve heard more friends – and commenters on Monevator – saying they’ve lost faith in UK state healthcare, for example, and so they’ve bolted on some kind of private provision.

Typically this is framed as an NHS issue – not enough resources from the left, too much waste from the right – but through another lens you might see a complex behemoth made for another era that’s buckling under modern demands.
Then we have, inevitably, AI, which is already overwhelming systems designed to serve citizens one posted envelope at a time.
With the concept of low-quality ‘AI slop’ now mainstream, organisations are sounding the alarm that their operations are being gummed up by ever greater volumes of correspondence.

These only take moments for users to create, but huge amounts of time for human employees to sift through and respond to. Bombarding public bodies with AI-generated requests has been labelled ‘agentic flooding’….
Perspective is required. If you think state capacity is fatally stretched in Europe and the US, you don’t want to see some of the other guys.

All the same, it’s another reason to try to ensure you can manage your own affairs as best you can. That’s always been the Monevator message when it comes to financial security, but the mindset might need to broaden.
Yes, it’s a privilege to have the option. But we can only meet the game as we find it.
Collapse, Big Brother, and other worst-case scenarios
A cohort of our fellow citizens is cheering along a breakdown of law, order, and the Internet.
Oh – they may concede the Mad Max horror show we’d face after such collapse could be unpleasant. But at least they’d have the consolation of being proven right.
I’m not going to dwell on the tail risks for life as we know it. Those guys have been at it for decades. They can get you up to speed, if you like.
With that said, long-term readers may recall I’ve long advocated thinking at least a bit about what I call Plan B or a ‘bug-out plan’.

Western nations have proven more than capable of the kind of self-harm we might have hoped was in the history books. For me, a second passport is now a must. Ideally you’d have some emergency assets offshore, too.
Of course you’d hope none of this was ever needed. Would you want to leave your friends and family behind if they hadn’t made similar provisions?
And again, frying pans and fires come to mind.
Get too paranoid and you’ll never feel secure. Witness the world’s richest men building bunkers in Nevada and New Zealand. When they’ve done one, I imagine they start on a backup.
Still, to think such stuff is, well, unthinkable, is a very Anglospheric perspective.
Look across the globe, and you’ll see the countries that escaped revolution, occupation, or a coup over the past century are more exceptions than the norm.
To conclude, let’s have a hearty two and a half cheers for everything working typically exactly as we’d expect it to each day.

I wake up in my cosy home and switch on my laptop. Almost always it’s all systems go. I earn a living without having to go through my front door, let alone putting up with bullshit office life or an expensive and miserable commute. And some of the money I make is diverted to an all-but-free index fund that gives me a growing stake in the progress of Earth PLC without me lifting a finger.
It’s an age of miracle and wonder, as Paul Simon sang in his own miraculous and wondrous era 40 years ago. And he probably didn’t even have a mobile phone.
Let’s hope things continue to mostly work. But let’s not be complacent, eh?
